title: Faster Discovery of Faster System Configurations with Spectral Learning

edges.target: Siegmund et al. FW/PW/HO/HS feature-interaction sampling (SPLConqueror)
edges.ref: [39] Siegmund, Kolesnikov, Kastner, Apel, Batory, Rosenmuller, Saake. Predicting performance via automated feature-interaction detection. ICSE 2012.
edges.evidence: the FW heuristic of Siegmund et al. ... has the higher errors rate and the highest standard deviation on that error rate (four out of six times). Hence, we cannot recommend this method

edges.target: Guo et al. progressive random sampling + CART (2N, PW)
edges.ref: [18] Guo, Czarnecki, Apel, Siegmund, Wasowski. Variability-aware performance prediction: A statistical learning approach. ASE 2013.
edges.evidence: As to the approach of Guo et al. (with PW), it does not standout on any of our measurements ... its standard deviations are usually larger and it requires much more data than WHAT

edges.target: Sarkar et al. projective / cost-efficient sampling
edges.ref: [34] Sarkar, Guo, Siegmund, Apel, Czarnecki. Cost-efficient sampling for performance prediction of configurable systems. ASE 2015.
edges.evidence: Although the approach of Sarkar et al. produces an error rate that is sometimes less than the one of WHAT, it requires the highest number of measurements ... we cannot recommend this approach

edges.target: Sarkar et al. reported low mean error rates
edges.ref: [34] Sarkar, Guo, Siegmund, Apel, Czarnecki. Cost-efficient sampling for performance prediction of configurable systems. ASE 2015.
edges.evidence: Our low mu values are consistent with prior work [34]

edges.target: Configurable-system performance datasets (Apache, BDBC, BDBJ, LLVM, SQLite, x264)
edges.ref: [39] Siegmund et al. Predicting performance via automated feature-interaction detection. ICSE 2012 (data via PROMISE openscience repo)
edges.evidence: We evaluated our approach on six real-world configurable software systems borrowed from the literature ... all the data used in this work are available on-line in the PROMISE code repository

edges.target: WHERE spectral clusterer (Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [29] Menzies, Butcher, Cok, Marcus, Layman, Shull, Turhan, Zimmermann. Local versus global lessons for defect prediction and effort estimation. TSE 39(6), 2013.
edges.evidence: WHERE = PDDP - PCA + FASTMAP; WHAT = WHERE + {S1, S2, S3} + CART ... all our algorithms are on-line at github.com/ai-se/where

edges.target: FASTMAP (Faloutsos and Lin)
edges.ref: [14] Faloutsos, Lin. Fastmap: A fast algorithm for indexing, data-mining and visualization of traditional and multimedia datasets. SIGMOD 1995.
edges.evidence: The FASTMAP method of Faloutsos and Lin [14], which rather than N^2 comparisons only performs 2N where N is the number of configurations

edges.target: PDDP principal direction divisive partitioning (Boley)
edges.ref: [4] Boley. Principal direction divisive partitioning. Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 2(4), 1998.
edges.evidence: A spectral-learning algorithm initially inspired by Boley's PDDP system [4], which we modify by replacing PCA with FASTMAP

edges.target: Platt: FASTMAP is a Nystrom approximation to first PCA component
edges.ref: [32] Platt. Fastmap, metricmap, and landmark mds are all nystrom algorithms. AISTATS 2005.
edges.evidence: which Platt has shown computes a Nystrom approximation to the first component of PCA [32]

edges.target: CART regression trees (Breiman et al.)
edges.ref: [5] Breiman, Friedman, Stone, Olshen. Classification and Regression Trees. CRC, 1984.
edges.evidence: we use a CART regression-tree learner [5] to build a performance predictor

edges.target: scikit-learn
edges.ref: [31] Pedregosa et al. Scikit-learn: Machine learning in Python. JMLR 12, 2011.
edges.evidence: we took care to either clearly define our algorithms or use implementations from the public domain (SciKitLearn) [31]

edges.target: GALE optimizer (Krall, Menzies, Davies)
edges.ref: [26] Krall, Menzies, Davies. Gale: Geometric active learning for search-based software engineering. TSE 41(10), 2015.
edges.evidence: related that baseline to three optimizers (GALE [26], DE [40] and NSGA-II [9]) using their default parameters

edges.target: Differential Evolution (Storn and Price)
edges.ref: [40] Storn, Price. Differential evolution - a simple and efficient heuristic for global optimization over continuous spaces. J Global Optim 11(4), 1997.
edges.evidence: we run the model (generated by WHAT + S1) against other optimizers, such as NSGA-II and differential evolution [40]

edges.target: NSGA-II (Deb et al.)
edges.ref: [9] Deb, Pratap, Agarwal, Meyarivan. A fast and elitist multiobjective genetic algorithm: NSGA-II. TEC 6(2), 2002.
edges.evidence: related that baseline to three optimizers (GALE [26], DE [40] and NSGA-II [9]) using their default parameters

edges.target: Bootstrap significance test (Efron and Tibshirani)
edges.ref: [13] Efron, Tibshirani. An Introduction to the Bootstrap. CRC, 1994.
edges.evidence: For testing statistical significance, we used non-parametric bootstrap test 95% confidence [13]

edges.target: A12 effect size (Vargha and Delaney)
edges.ref: [42] Vargha, Delaney. A critique and improvement of the CL common language effect size statistics of McGraw and Wong. JEBS 25(2), 2000.
edges.evidence: followed by an A12 test to check that any observed differences were not trivially small effects ... (as per Vargha [42], we say that a 'small' effect has a < 0.6)

edges.target: Scott-Knott ranking (Mittas and Angelis)
edges.ref: [30] Mittas, Angelis. Ranking and clustering software cost estimation models through a multiple comparisons algorithm. TSE 39(4), 2013.
edges.evidence: we use the Scott-Knott test to recursively divide our optimizers ... This use of Scott-Knott is endorsed by Mittas and Angelis [30]

edges.target: Scott-Knott usage in SE (Ghotra, McIntosh, Hassan)
edges.ref: [16] Ghotra, McIntosh, Hassan. Revisiting the impact of classification techniques on the performance of defect prediction models. ICSE 2015.
edges.evidence: This use of Scott-Knott is endorsed by Mittas and Angelis [30] and by Hassan et al. [16]

edges.target: Correlation dimension (Grassberger and Procaccia)
edges.ref: [17] Grassberger, Procaccia. Measuring the strangeness of strange attractors. Physica D 9(1-2), 1983.
edges.evidence: we borrow the concept of correlation dimension from the domain of physics [17] ... we estimate the intrinsic dimensionality as the mean slope between ln(C(r)) and ln(r)

edges.target: Kamvar et al. definition of 'spectral learner'
edges.ref: [25] Kamvar, Klein, Manning. Spectral learning. IJCAI 2003.
edges.evidence: Hence, this method is a 'spectral clusterer' in the general Kamvar sense. Note that, for our data, we have not found that Kamvar's normalization matrices are needed.

edges.target: Xu et al.: developers ignore 5/6ths of configuration options
edges.ref: [44] Xu, Jin, Fan, Zhou, Pasupathy, Talwadker. Hey, you have given me too many knobs! FSE 2015.
edges.evidence: developers tend to ignore over 5/6ths of the configuration options, which leaves considerable optimization potential untapped and induces major economic cost [44]

edges.target: Zhang et al. Fourier learning sample-size result
edges.ref: [46] Zhang, Guo, Blais, Czarnecki. Performance prediction of configurable software systems by fourier learning. ASE 2015.
edges.evidence: While a theoretically satisfying result, that approach still needs thousands to hundreds of thousands of executions of sample configurations

edges.target: O(N^2) cost of standard PCA/spectral methods (Ilin and Raiko)
edges.ref: [23] Ilin, Raiko. Practical approaches to principal component analysis in the presence of missing values. JMLR 11, 2010.
edges.evidence: a standard spectral method requires an O(N^2) matrix multiplication to compute the components of PCA [23]

edges.target: Siegmund et al. internal/external validity framing
edges.ref: [37] J. Siegmund, N. Siegmund, Apel. Views on internal and external validity in empirical software engineering. ICSE 2015.
edges.evidence: Validity refers to the extent to which a piece of research actually investigates what the researcher purports to investigate [37]

edges.target: Burges: modeling in low intrinsic-dimension manifolds is easier
edges.ref: [6] Burges. Dimension reduction: A guided tour. Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 2(4), 2010.
edges.evidence: Our results are inline with the observation made by Bruges, as we show that few samples are enough to model a large (sometimes millions) space

edges.target: Domingos: curse of dimensionality / blessing of non-uniformity
edges.ref: [11] Domingos. A few useful things to know about machine learning. CACM 55(10), 2012.
edges.evidence: Domingos [11] explains how our intuitions fail in higher dimensions ... what counteracts this is the 'blessing of non-uniformity'

edges.target: Chen et al.: Euclidean distance may miss most-dissimilar points
edges.ref: [7] Chen, Nair, Krishna, Menzies. Is 'sampling' better than 'evolution' for search-based software engineering? arXiv:1608.07617, 2016.
edges.evidence: there maybe systems where Euclidean distance (as used in this paper) cannot find the most dissimilar points [7]. For such systems, WHAT in current form will not be effective

not_reuse_examples: [38] Siegmund et al. 2015 performance-influence models: explicitly NOT compared ('we did not compare our work to performance-influence models'); related-work mention only.
[36] Shi and Malik normalized cuts: cited to contrast WHAT with image-processing spectral clustering; nothing adopted or run.
[15] Fletcher / [20] Harman et al.: cited only as pointers to 'hundreds of other optimizers'; no method taken.
[1,2,10,45] Bettenburg, Deiters, Zhang: 'use of underlying dimension has been endorsed by' — background endorsement, nothing reused.
notes: Method paper (WHAT spectral sampler, arXiv 2017 / EMSE-style); heavy self-reuse (Siegmund/Apel baselines + datasets, Menzies WHERE/GALE); Fig 7 caption miscites 'Arcuri and Briand ICSE 11' as [30] (actually Mittas & Angelis); data both 'borrowed from the literature' and 'we ran all configurations', so dataset executed=true with transitive PROMISE-repo origin.
